I do not know where they got it, hut they have it. Now, the hon. member for St. Antoine has given a very lucid and concise account of the position in which we stand under this proposed legislation. But I may summarize the matter in this way. As 1 have said, we are relying now entirely on the guarantee of the Grand Trunk Railway Company. We have the Finance Minister admitting first the prior lien of $121,000,000 in respect of the debenture stock; second, I think I have proved that rentals capitalized are a prior lien amounting to $19,000,000; third, the debenture stock authorized to be issued this session amounts to $12,000,000 and will be a prior lien. This makes a total of $152,000,000 of undoubted prior incumbrance. Then, if I am right in my assumption, according to Poor's Railway Manual, the Grand Trunk have the right to buy in with their debenture bonds these outlying railway stocks of railways purchased by them, and pay for them with debenture bonds of the Grand Trunk Railway. That would place another $75,000,000 of a prior incumbrance over our guarantee-total $227,568,000. Now, I want to ask the Finance Minister one more question. I notice that in the Act of 1862 and subsequent Acts, there are what are called equipment mortgage bonds, which are also said to be a prior incumbrance against the Grand Trunk Railway. I refer to page 783 of Poor's Manual, 1908, which says:
Perpetual 5 per cent, debenture stock (Grand Trunk section).-Created under powers of the company's Consolidated Debenture Stoolc Act, 1874, passed May 26, 1874. Secured by first mortgage on all the company's property, as also upon the company's interest in the International Bridge and in leased and operated lines, subject, however, to the priorities of all other preferential charges existing at date of issue; ranks immediately after the equipment mortgage bonds; interest 5 per cent, per annum, in perpetuity, payable January and July.
Either that authority is entirely wrong, cr the Finance Minister is wrong. I would like the hon. minister (Mr Fielding) to tell ns, whether in addition to the items I have mentioned, there is not also what is known ss the equipment mortgage bonds of some $6,000,000 outstanding as a preferential

claim, not merely to our guarantee but to the debenture stock referred to by the Finance Minister. If some of these bonds are not a prior lien, then Poor's Manual is wrong. The items I have mentioned amount to $233,000,000. As the hon. member for St. Antoine has pointed out, the Grand Trunk Railway have also guaranteed something like $50,000,000. We stand in the same position vith respect to our $10,000,000 as the other guarantors do with reference to the other $50,000,000-that is, we are in no better position than they are, and all stand subsequent to the above prior lien. Not only that, but the Grand Trunk may hereafter mortgage their property and make another prior lien and they may contract other obligations, and these will also rank pari passu with our own. I would like to know whether, under these circumstances, the Finance Minister thinks the loan that is being made is sufficiently secured by the guarantee of the Grand Trunk? You can judge what the company will do by what it has done. And what is our position? At confederation, according to the information brought down, the Grand Trunk owed us over $15,000,000 of principal and $10,000,000 of interest, a total of $25,000,000 and over, That amount has been owing for forty-two years. Forty-two years' interest at 4 per cent would amount to $43,000,000, which added to the amount already stated makes a total of $68,000,000 which the Grand Trunk owes us to-day. Have we any reason to suppose that they will repay us the present loan any more rapidly than they paid the old loan, unless we force from them further and other security than that which the government are getting from the company? That remained from confederation down to 1884, and in that year an Act was passed to the following effect, chapter 52, section 19, whereby it was enacted:
That the claim of the Dominion of Canada as it now1 exists. . . . shall rank after the common stock, and securities heretofore issued and authorized to be issued, and after the securities and common stock hereby authorized to be created.
Now where do we stand with respect to that? The consolidated debenture stock is $121,000,000; rentals capitalized, $19,000,000;
4 per cent guaranteed stock, $49,000,000; first preferred stock, $17,000,000; second preferred stock, $12,000,000; third preferred stock, $35,000,000; ordinary stock, $112,000,000. That makes $257,000,000 that is ahead of the debt of Canada to-day with respect to this $68,000,000. Then add to that the $75,000,000 of other stocks of this railway which the country has a right to purchase, add to that the debenture stock authorized this session but not issued, $12,003,000, and you have $344,000,000 standing ahead of this $68,000,000 which this company has owed the Dominion of Canada since 1867.

Now with respect to the loan of 1885, we are in the proud position of saying that every statement which we made then has been verified. Time has amply justified the assertions which we made, because we took precautions to take sufficient direct security from the Canadian Pacific Railway, and it was to their interest to pay it back again. With respect .to the contract of 1903 and 1904, on the contrary, every statement which the government made at that time has turned out to be false. They told us, for instance, that the eastern section would cost $71,000,000, they said they had mountains of information on which to base that calculation. But we find that section now is costing $124,000,000. They told us the mountain section would cost $26,000,000; we find that to-day, because oE the extra mileage and extra cost of construction, it is estimated to cost $67,000,000. With respect to the prairie section we find that they are coming back and asking for $10,003,000 more to complete that. So practically every statement	which they
made in 1904 has turned out to be absolutely falsified by the facts, and practically every statement made by the Conservatives at that time h s turned out to be true. As for the mountain section and the eastern section we have so far only estimates, and there is no prospect that these estimates will fully cover the amount required to be expended. Under these circumstances we of the opposition feel that we are entitled to the fullest information with regard to these stocks I have mentioned, and I would like the Finance Minister to tell the House whether these extra securities are a preferential claim over the whole guarantee. The members on this side of the House, I understand, do not propose to move any specific amendment to this resolution at this stage, but they propose to reserve their ammunition, and their judgment as to what step they will take when the Bill has been introduced and is being discussed on the second reading. We have done sufficiently tonight to show that practically every prediction the government has made has turned out to be untrue, ana therefore we are justified in proceeding with the utmost caution in granting this loan to the Grand Trunk Pacific.

Hon. gentlemen on the government side who have spoken in favour of the proposed loan of $10,000,000 to the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company, have dwelt at length upon the resources and importance of our west, and of the necessity of affording that country ample railway facilities. The hon. member for West Lambton (Mr. Pardee) read to the House a long list of figures showing the amount of gra:n produced in the west,
and he endeavoured to leave the impression on the House that the members of the opposition were opposed to giving the necessary railway facilities to the west to enable them to take their produce to market. Permit me to say that in my opinion the hon. members on this side of the House have quite as much faith in the future of the west as have hon. members supporting the government. We are ready to assist any effort to give the necessary railway facilities for handling the increasing products of that portion of our country. It would not be in keeping with the traditions of the Conservative party, the party that laid the foundation of the present transportation system in the west by building the Canadian Pacific Railway, were we to place any obstruction in the way of the further development of the west by the buildings of more railways. True, the Conservative party did oppose, and strongly oppose, in 1903 and 1904, the policy of the government in connection with the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company, and I think that subsequent events have justified the Conservative party in taking the position they did at that time. While some arguments may be advanced in support of that portion of the line from Winnipeg to Quebec, if we consider the nature of the country through which that road passes, the great expenditure that will be necessary for maintenance and keeping up the staff on that part of the road during the winter season, also the fact that during the summer season that road will have to compete with navigation, I fail to see how that portion of the road can be made to pay. As for that part of the road which runs from Quebec to. Moncton, I have never yet heard a reasonable argument advanced in support of its construction. It practically parallels the Intercolonial, with which it will have to compete. The Intercolonial at present does not pay running expenses, without taking into account any charge for interest on the capital invested. The Grand Trunk Railway Company, in 1903, being anxious to extend their system into the west, approached this government and sought to obtain a charter authorizing them to build a line of railway from North Bay west. Had that proposition been taken up we have reason to believe that at the present time the Grand Trunk Railway Company would be in a very good position to handle its share of the western trade. The government did not look favourably upon that proposal, and they substituted the present Grand Trunk Pacific Railway scheme. That scheme was strongly opposed by the then Minister of Railways, a very able gentleman, the one man in the cabinet who was in the best position to judge of the meT-

its of the proposition. The hon. leader of the opposition "when this resolution was before the House a week ago, submitted a statement showing that under the terms of the contract this country will be called upon to pay at least $40,000,000 for interest alone, before the Grand Trunk Railway Company, under their contract, will be called upon to pay rent for the eastern section of the road. That is an amount about three times as much as the total cost of the road was estimated by the First Minister when this proposition was first placed before the House. We were told by the present hon. Minister of the Interior (Mr.- Oliver) in 1904 that the Domiinon of Canada was bonus-ing this railway to the extent of from $12,000,000 to $20,000,000. In view of the information now before the House, it appears to me that the minister will require to revise his estimate. Although the Grand Trunk Pacific scheme may have been a mistake we are in this position at the present time; the country by the contract it has entered into and in consequence of having given its credit, is bound to see that road completed even although it may have been a mistake in the first place. So, the question for us to consider at the present time is what is the best course to pursue to secure the completion of the road. The Grand Trunk Railway Company have approached the government and have asked that the terms of the contract be varied by this government loaning them $10,000,000. During this present session of parliament we have heard the hon. member for Strath-cona (Mr. McIntyre) and, I think also, the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Turriff) advance the argument that when a great Tailway corporation comes to this government and seeks special legislation this government should avail itself of the opportunity to secure better terms from that company. That was the argument advanced by these hon. members when the question of authorizing the issue of $50,000,000 of additional stock in connection with the Canadian Pacific Railway was before the House. It does appear to me that this would be an opportune time for this government to put that policy into effect and to say to the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company:	'If
you are prepared, under the terms of the contract to go on and complete the road, all well and good; if you are not prepared under the contract to go on and complete the road, then we will take over the road, we will reimburse you your expenditure so far and complete the road, and own, not only the lean eastern section but also the western section which, it is expected, will prove profitable.'
There is no question but that it is absolutely necessary for ue to go on and complete this Grand Trunk Pacific Railway. That rvas settled in 1903 and 1904.

I did not intend saying anything this evening, and in what I shall say, I shall speak unly for myself. I have listened with great -attention to the speeches delivered from this side, and have been thoroughly convinced, from the evidence and arguments presented to us, that this resolution is very defective, and that, if it is to become the basis of a Bill, which will involve this country in an expenditure of $10,000,000, it should be greatly re-arranged and remodelled. In its present shape, I cannot see my way to support it. In common with other hon. members on this side

I am quite in favour of our finishing the road. Canada is committed to the building of the Grand Trunk Pacific and that road must be completed. But if we continue to waste our money and misappropriate the funds of the country, as we appear to be doing under this resolution, the road will never be finished. Why, that part of the line between Winnipeg and Edmonton, is simply to be built over the prairie. There are no very high grades in all that distance! and very few curves. There is not timber to get out of the way and the right of way can be very cheaply obtained, so that the line should not cost more than $15,000 a mile. Other railways in the United States and Canada have been built for that price through very similar sections. Now we provided the Grand Trunk Pacific with $13,000 a mile to begin with and they are coming back to us for $10,000,000 more or nearly $10,000 per mile in addition. Certainly any one could build a railway if he had such backing. There is not a man in this House who could not build the whole railway between Winnipeg and Edmonton, if he had such backing that he did not require himself to put a dollar into it. But if we are to have this trouble with the prairie section, where will the money come from to finish the mountain and the eastern section ? If it costs that much to build over the level prairie, what will it cost when we have to cut through miles of solid rock in the mountains of British Columbia ? The country, at this rate, will not only be ruined, but will never get the road. It is not too late for the government to reconsider the matter and make some change in this resolution. We wish to see the resolution get through and the road built, but we want to have some security for our money; and after the evidence presented to this House to-night by the hon. member for St. Antoine division (Mr. Ames) the hon. member from North Grey (Mr. Middlebro) and the hon. member for South Bruce (Mr. Donnelly), I must say that it seems to me we are getting no security at all for our $10,000,000.
If we are to become bankers for this company, we ought to act as bankers would. When I go to a bank for a loan, they look very carefully into the security I offer. They expect me to be able to show that I am worth the money I am asking for and a good deal more. Well, if we are to be bankers in one sense, we ought to act as bankers in another sense. When I go to a bank for a loan, the banker has the money and does not need to go and borrow it. In this case Canada has not the money herself. She must go to Europe to borrow before she can loan it. Any one could set up as a banker if he had credit. He could loan money to all his neighbours and make hosts of friends if he had the privilege of borrowing the money Mb. THOS. CHISHOLM.
and the credit of the country to back him. It would have been quite time enough for the _ government to go into the banking business when able to pay their own debts. I am sorry, under the circumstances, that I have to express myself in this manner; but unless this resolution be changed very much I shall have to vote against it.

I would like to put a question to the hon. the Minister of Finance. I find that in his speech the other day he said-page 3676 of ' Hansard ':
Therefore we admit that in giving the company the benefit of this loan, we are taking at par a security which they could not float at par, and giving them the benefit of 4 per cent though they themselves could not borrow at that rate, and the government has recently had to pay over 4 per cent.
I would like to ask the hon. minister what earthly reason there is why we should lend this money to the Grand Trunk Pacific at a less rate of interest than we have to pay?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It does not follow that we are lending at a less rate of interest than we have to pay, because if the money has to be borrowed, it is possible that it will he borrowed at less than 4 per cent, and if so, we would make a profit. However, even if we were giving them an advantage to that extent it would be a relief to the company. A number of questions of a legal character have been asked this evening which I would not undertake to answer off hand. They are worthy of consideration, and if they justify further inquiry, we must take them into account. But what Impresses my mind is that these securities which we propose to take, whatever their rank and standing may be, have at this moment a money value in the markets of the world to the extent of 90 per cent. Some of the securities were recently issued at 90 per cent.
With 70 per cent of them left on the hands of the underwriters.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Some of the best loans are left in the hands of the underwriters. But I say that the risk we take in this matter is the risk of the margin, which is roughly speaking about 10 per cent. We could put these securities on the money market to-day, and realize 90 per cent of their face value, probably with some charges for financing.
Could the company float the loan at 90 per cent?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I think probably they could not have done so a month ago, but there has since been an improvement in the condition of the money market. It is not worth while arguing as to the rank and priority of these securities. All

these matters have been known and taken into consideration by the financiers who have fixed the value of the property, and that is roughly to-day 90 per cent.

The hon. minister's argument has put a completely different face on the question. We have been asked to grant this loan as a measure of relief to the company. That is the whole burden of the final portion of Mr. Hays' letter. As a banking transaction, it has not very much to commend it. But if the company could float these bonds with only 10 per cent reduction, we do not need to come to their help.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I think we do. I think the flotation of these securities at a very low price would affect the character of the enterprise and the character and standing of the company generally. The measure of risk we are taking is roughly speaking about 10 per cent. I do not hesitate to say that the value of these securities is to be found chiefly in the guarantee of the Grand Trunk Railway Company of Canada. The mortgage security will have some value in the future. To my mind it is not of great value to-day, though as the years roll on, it will be more valuable. But with the guarantee of the Grand Trunk Railway Company of Canada, while the money market to-day would not have faith enough in these securities to take them at par, the improving conditions of the whole enterprise as the work goes on, as the road is put into operation through the prairie and other sections, as the country improves, as business improves, as money becomes easier, we have faith that these securities will be worth one hundred cents on the dollar, and on that faith we accept them. The amount at risk is simply the margin between the par value of the securities and what they might be sold for in the money market to-day. I admit that if they were sold to-day, they would have to be sold at a sacrifice, but we ask the House to adopt this measure on the faith that when the loan falls due they will be worth one hundred cents on the dollar, and therefore we are risking nothing.

Do I understand the hon. minister to say that the bonds to be given to the government for the loan will be the same as those placed on the market at 90 a little while ago by the underwriters and not taken up by the public?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I do not attach much importance to the question whether they were taken up by the public or not; but I said they are substantially of the same character, inasmuch as they are bonds of the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company guaranteed by the Grand Trunk Railway Company of Canada. The man who promises to pay and the man who endorses are practically the same in both cases. As to their precise rank and standing, I do not see that it is important.

The bond that.was placed on the London market was a second mortgage bond, while the bond the government is now taking is a fourth mortgage bond. The mortgage given to secure the second mortgage bond has a substantial value- although it was not taken up by the public at 90-because it is not only a second mortgage immediately after the government guarantee, but it has special privileges in case there is default. It ranks largely in the same category as the first mortgage bonds. Therefore I ask the hon. minister whether it is not true that the mortgage securing the second mortgage bonds has a substantial value far and away in excess of any possible value of the mortgage securing this loan?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I do not attach as much importance to the point as my hon. friend seems to do. I think that in all these securities, the real thing to the investor is the guarantee of the Grand Trunk Railway Company of Canada. As to the other securities, my hon. friend is wrong. The securities I referred to were not second mortgage bonds, but the equipment lien established by statute. If you call that a mortgage, it was a third and not a second. But for all present purposes the valuable security is the guarantee of the Grand Trunk Company. The other securities will have value in the future.
However, according to what the minister has said they are putting a first mortgage on the rolling stock.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No, the rolling stock is really included in the first mortgage.
No, I think the minister is mistaken, the Act distinctly stated that the first mortgage did not cover the rolling stock.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I think it does although a special security was created to raise the money; I think it was all included in fire first mortgage.
Mr. PERLEY I think the hon. minister is mistaken.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I find that the equipment is included in the first mortgage.
The equipment and the rolling stock are different propositions altogether.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I do not know about that.

Certainly they are.

The rolling stock is a separate account.

As I understand it this third mortgage, that is the loan of the 25th of February, 1909, which was issued in London, and of which 77i per cent was left on the hands of the underwriters, had by way of security the rolling stock, and after that came what equity was left after previous liens on the property of the Grand Trunk Pacific beside the guarantee of the Grand Trunk and that loan we know was a drug on the market. speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: My hon. friend will find that equipment, meaning rolling stock, is embraced in the first mortgage and that their success in the market was due to the guarantee of the Grand Trunk; practically that money was raised on the security of the Grand Trunk. Am I correct in understanding that if we grant this $10,000,000 loan, $7,000,000 of it will be used in paying moneys advanced by the Grand Trunk and that therefore there will only be $3,000,000 left for the purpose of pushing on the work?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: In a sense that is correct. We, of course, will not pay it to the Grand Trunk; it must be paid out to the Grand Trunk Pacific Eailway Company, upon the certificates of the engineer; but we do know as a matter of fact that the Grand Trunk Eailway has advanced out of its treasury a considerable sum of money and that the $7,000,000 which they have used to assist this work will be returned to them indirectly. We will not pay it to them, but we will pay it upon certificates showing that this money has gone into the work. No doubt the Grand Trunk Pacific will pay that back into the treasury of the Grand Trunk Eailway, to which it properly belongs. [DOT]
Will that be paid on certificates for work already done or for work which is yet to be done?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Of course we cannot pay out money upon any future work to be done; we can only pay it upon certificates for work already actually done.
Mr. AMES
At the time you paid?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes, and if they have already done that work and can furnish certificates to show that amount of money has in all good faith gone into the work, we can pay the amount. We will pay it to the Grand Trunk Pacific in the usual way dnd they having got money to do this work from the treasury of the Grand Trunk of Canada will, I presume, pay it back to that company. That is a transaction between the two companies. We will only pay upon the certificate of the engineer that the work has been done and the money expended according to the representations made.

Has the minister reason to believe that $3,000,000 will relieve their present financial embarrassment and enable them to push on the work rapidly until completion? It would seem to me such a small amount, having regard to the mileage yet to be built, that I would expect to find them in financial difficulties again before the summer is out and another application made for aid. What have the government done to satisfy themselves that they will be able, when this is advanced, to go on and complete the work within a reasonable time?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The government engineer certifies that this $10,000,000-there is a slight difference between the estimates of the railway and the government engineers-will complete the prairie section.
Have you any guarantee that the builders of the mountain section will not be back for aid?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I do not know. Sufficient unto the day is the good thereof.
What government engineers have given this estimate and certificate?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The estimates were prepared naturally by the engineers of the Grand Trunk Pacific when they made their application. Their estimates were referred to Mr. Schreiber, the government engineer, and he has made a report which will be found among the papers brought down.

I have looked over a few of his estimates and have had occasion to inquire into some certificates before and I must confess from my experience in regard to these, that I would not attach the very highest values to a certificate from that source.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I would say in that respect that all engineers are human and imperfect and the best of them will make mistakes. It must be remembered that the Grand Trunk Pacific Co. are constructing the prairie section of the road and not the government. Hon. members speak of the excessive cost of the eastern division as some

thing for which the government are to be blamed, but the prairie section is being constructed by the Grand Trunk Pacific, with the aid of the Grand Trunk, with all the paraphernalia of the Grand Trunk engineers, and we are told that the Grand Trunk and the Grand Trunk Pacific are rather severe in their dealings with contractors and employees, so there is no reason to doubt that every effort has been made to make the cost of the prairie section as reasonable as possible. Thus when we find that this road is being constructed by the railway company without any interference by the government, except supervision, and that this largely increased cost is rendered necessary, it should show my hon. friends that the increase must be for good and sufficient reasons. With regard to Mr. Schreiber's renorts all engineers are human, and it is only fair to Mr. Schreiber, an old engineer who has been in the service of the country for a very long time, to say that although he may make mistakes, all who know him will feel that any estimate and report which he makes is made in the light of a long experience, in the light of the knowledge of a trained and very able engineer, and of an experience which I am sure we all recognize as the experience of a man who has, in the fullest degree, the confidence and respect of all who know him.

I would like very much to share in that opinion, but I frankly confess I do not and I think we have had sufficient evidence to justify a different opinion altogether. But if there was nothing else in the situation beyond the fact that the first estimates of the cost of this road and the second are so different, it would be quite sufficient to justify us in having very serious doubts as to whether the same thing would not occur with subsequent estimates. The experience of the past does not justify any strong ground for the belief that the present estimate is not likely to prove'inaccurate just as well as the estimates which have been made up to the present.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It is our only means of judging, the estimate of a reputable engineer.

Talking about reputable engineers, I do not wish to do Mr. Schreiber any injustice in the world, but I frankly confess that I believe the government could get him to give an estimate to suit their own purposes on any subject.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
My hon. friend must be speaking of former times and other governments. I can only say that I have ever found Mr. Schreiber a most faithful and efficient public servant, and I never knew a man who would dare to suggest to him an estimate -which did not respond
in every way to his own conviction of what was right.

Do we require any better evidence than the contract of M. P. Davis, on the Cornwall canal? Under his own hand, Mr. Schreiber said that the amount was a proper one, that it was reasonable, and recommended to the Minister of Railways that it be paid. And the Minister of Railways did the same. But the Auditor General stood out, declaring that he would not pay it, because it was rank robbery. And the amount was reduced from $52,000 to $29,000-and this the Auditor General said was- $10,000 too much-and it was accepted as payment in full.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I do not remember the details of the Davis case. But any man who knows Mr. Schreiber will believe that any estimate he ever gave was given in the most perfect good faith and that it was an estimate the government would have a right to accept as being that of an engineer of high reputation and ripe experience.
What was his estimate of the cost of the mountain division?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I do not recollect.
Thirty thousand dollars a mile, was it not?	.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I cannot recall it.
And now it is estimated at $80,000. That is very accurate for an engineer, is it not?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The conditions governing the cost of public works have changed enormously since that time. The very fact that the prairie section has proven so much more costly than was estimated-
Why?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: For fifty reasons.
Give us forty-nine of them.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: If time permits, I will give, later on, not only forty-nine but the whole fifty. Does not the hon. gentleman (Mr. Hughes) know that labour costs more than it did?
No.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I know it.
No, the hon. minister will pardon me-he does not know it.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I did not go out to pay the bills, but I have the reports of men who did, and I am satisfied and believe
I know all about it.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The hon. gentleman cannot know much more about it than I do. He gets his knowledge from other people, just as I do. But I state, from the best information I have been able to obtain, that the cost of labour is very much in excess of what it was.
And what else?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The rates paid for ties have doubled.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Because the men who cut the ties are getting higher wages. Go into the steel mills and ask in the office there why the road is costing more and they will tell you-it is because their men are getting better wages.
Oh, oh.
What are the rails today?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I have the floor.
I would like to ask

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons

speechtext: I say, go into the steel mills, and they will tell you

they will tell you
that their men are getting higher wages. The workmen who cut the ties are getting higher wages. Go into the contractor's office, and he will tell you that he is getting two prices where he got one before.

Now, Colonel, what is it ?
In the first place, Mr. Chairman, I would ask you to call the minister to order for not addressing the chair ?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is right, I apologize.

Let me tell the Finance Minister that it is true that ties to-day are deareT when placed on the track, but they are not dearer in the woods. There is Mr. HUGHES.
what we want to get at. Why should there be this increased cost between, the woods and the placing in the track. Rails are about as cheap as they were in 1904-I do not know but what they are a little cheaper.
They are cheaper.

I believe that they are cheaper than when this contract was made. The wages paid in this country are lower than they were when this contract was made. Why, the minister has only to take the case of the public works in the town of Lindsay. The contract there is not being carried out on the fair wage scale; the-prices paid by the contractor there are considerably lower than in any other industry in the town. If the Minister of Finance is going into these details, we want to get the facts, for, with the facts, we can prove him to be wrong ? Let him give the fifty reasons of which he has spoken.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I think that forty-nine will be quite enough to prove the hon. gentleman (Mr. Hughes) wrong.

On the National Transcontinental, where they pay foT ties from 60 cents to 75 cents, the man who cut the ties, perhaps only a hundred yards away, from where this price is given did not get more than one-quarter of that for them.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The men who buy the ties get them at the best price they can.
MQr. FOSTER. It would help us if we could get down to the facts with regard to even part of these fifty reasons, and the minister has an easy method of getting at the facts.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

If he will institute a little inquiry, he will find out the exact wages paid to the different grades of men in 1904, and he can find the scale ox wages paid to the same grades of men in 1907 and 1908. This would be something authentic. If we had also an authoritative statement of the cost of supplies in the different years, we could make a fair estimate of what was due to the increased cost in that regard. Then, as to rails, it would be easy for the Finance Minister to have the information for us as to what rails were sold at in 1904 and in 1908. These are stock articles, and the price can easily be ascertained. Information could be given us also as to the cost of ties. With these facts, we could get somewhere near the added cost. But has the Finance Minister looked into the particulars sufficiently to satisfy himself that $35,000 a mile could have been economically put into that road under its present construction? I have talked to men who have built railways through that country as well as through other sections, and the Minister of Finance ought to have had curiosity enough to make inquiries also. Other roads have been built in this prairie country-the Canadian Pacific Railway and the Canadian Northern are constantly building there. Has the minister made inquiry to find out what these other companies are paying per mile for the building of their roads? Has he that information on file? Before we come to the rescue by a ten-million dollar loan, ought we not to satisfy ourselves that there has not been rank extravagance-to speak of nothing else -in building that prairie section at a cost of $35,000 per mile? This amount, as I understand it, does not include equipment of rolling stock. Am I right in that ?

Grand Trunk Pacific. Are these things true? if they are, it is sufficient to make us sit up and think. You talk about the weary Titan, the old mother, but there is young Titan here whose back is being bent by the financial burdens that she is obliged to carry, and that young Titan is Canada itself. When we have to strain every nerve to get what wo want for our own purposes, we allow these men to skim all the cream off the Grand Trunk Pacific, perquisites, town sites, lumber business and a dozen others, and we patiently bend our backs and add to the financial burden that we find already more than we can carry. It is time we become sober with reference to the debt and the obligations which are being rolled' in upon this country. The Finance Minister comes to us and asks us for a loan. He is the man to give us the information. When we made a loan to the Canadian Pacific Railway we took a lien on their $35,000,000 of stock; the lien was a good lien and a strong lien for the $35,000,000. There is $35,000,000 of your stock, we want that as well/ and we took the loan upon that. But here, the company cannot offer us a security that is worth sixpence to this government. As the hon. Minister of Finance has said the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway gives its bond, but, as he says, its bond is not presently worth anything. We go to the Grand Trunk Railway Company which guarantees the bonds. That is really what we get. The Minister of Finance knows how much. He can tell us. These are some questions which the Minister of Finance should undertake to answer, and to answer, I think, before we get through with this measure. We are now approaching the Easter holidays-days of peace and calm after some little excitement of the past. We do not want to get into another exciting time before that gracious season comes on and so we cannot carry out all our wishes to-night with reference to this resolution. We are going to allow this resolution to pass through committee with the reservation that every line and sentence of it stands yet to be approved, or amended or approved with such emendation as we can get; but when the Bill, which is founded upon the resolution, comes down in de-Mr. FOSTER.
tail it can be taken up, acted upon and be amended much more easily than in the case of the resolution. But the Minister of Finance has to get more than forty-nine out of these fifty little reasons that he offered to the committee, and I am sure he will. There is another question that we want to get a little information on. How much money of the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company has gone into rolling stock? When did it go into that rolling stock ? Who has been using the rolling stock from that day to this? Is the rolling stock new or is it largely made up of repaired stock from another company and then taken as rolling stock into the Grand Trunk Pacific? We want to know why this new company, which has nothing to roll on, goes to work and spends, I do not know how many millions-the Minister of Finance knows-five, six, seven or eight millions-ton rolling stock long before it has anything upon which the stock can roll. The company may say that they must make some provision or else when they got the road they would have to wait some time longer, but there are two questions that suggest themselves: How long have they had that rolling stock? What has it been doing in the meantime. Has it simply been used as a convenience for the Grand Trunk Railway, or has it been fairly and squarely built and bought as the necessities of the Grand Trunk Pacific called for it? There is another question. Who constitutes the company that builds the rolling stock? We would like to know something about that part of the matter. It would be interesting to us and altogether germane because the Finance Minister himself does not want to ask that Canadian credit be strained to the amount of $10,000,000 unless everything is square and fair. We do not want to have it go unless it is square and fair and if it is not square and fair we would like to know it. We would all feel better if we did know it. Looking at the cream skimming propensity which has shown itself upon everything in sight along that Grand Trunk Pacific without one drop of that going into the parched and hungry mouth of the Grand Trunk Pacific Corporation itself, we are also anxious to know whether that is going on in the car building process. We would like to know something about the constitution of the car building company that is furnishing this stock. These are some of the questions which come to the surface. The Minister of Finance, I think, has not quite properly settled another. He pretty nearly cut the whole ground from under his feet when he declared that they could go into the market to-day and get 90 per cent, of these securities. Why in the world, under these circumstances and under our circumstances at the present time, should we not

allow this great company to take this discount of ten per cent and go on with this road? Other companies have to do it. There is not a railway company in this country of any size at all which has not had to submit to heavy discounts upon its stock and bonds. If what the Minister of Finance says is true it does not seem to me that there is any great necessity for us to put out neck under the yoke when we have already taken the heavy burden to draw and which we will have to draw. I do not know that it is necessary for me to make any other remarks at the present time but these are some of the things that I desire to bring to the attention of the minister. If this loan is necessary I say that the Minister of Finance has no business in a matter like this, after the regal support that we have given to this measure, when there is an emergency with reference to $10,000,000 of stock, to make another gift. Let them pay exactly the interest that we pay. I do not ask that they should pay more, but let him make his proposition so that he will exact in interest what the $10,000,000 costs us. At least I think that ought to be done. Why should we act the part of the beneficent mother to any greater extent than we have, for no man will deny that so far Canada, forced through it and into it by the government, has lifted and is to-day lifting nearly 90 per cent of the whole load. We will take other times to discuss this question and when the Bill comes on, founded upon this resolution, we will have something further to say, but these are some of the things that we were anxious to know about and things which, before the Bill gets through, we must know about. I am not satisfied at all as to the evidence we have of the $35,000 a mile that went into the road. I am not at all satisfied, and I think there ought to be some further research into that before we let it pass; my hon. friend the Finance Minister can get at that much better than any one else because he has all the sources at his command.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
My hon. friends opposite are rather hard to please. At the beginning of this matter, my hon. friend the leader of the opposition, framed a series of questions for the purpose of eliciting all 1301
the information he thought was necessary to enable the House to enter upon an intelligent study of this transaction. I thought that many of his questions did not have much bearing on the resolution; but as nevertheless they did have some_ relation to the Grand Trunk Pacific project generally, we brought down all the information desired. I think that in almost every instance everything my hon. friend sought was granted. But now we find my hon. friend from North Toronto speaking as if there were some dreadful neglect in supply ing information.

I would not say neglect. So. faT I think my hon. friend has come up to the requirements very well indeed, but what I am now making is not a charge of neglect,, but a modest request for some further information, because as the discussion proceeds other points arise which require elucidation.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Very much of the information the hon. gentleman desires is ' asked for in so indefinite and hazy a way that it may be difficult to give it precise form. If my hon. friends had framed their questions in a precise form as did the leader of the opposition, I should make every effort to comply, but it is rather difficult to know exactly what it is they do require. My hon. friend from North Tor-on (Mr. Foster) is very prolific in 'ifs'. It is very easy to found an argument on 'ifs.' If this is the fact and that is the case, and if something else occurs, then something else is bound to result. One can build a monument of arguments on an 'if.' I would be glad to understand what the hon. gentleman means by this cream skimming operation which he says, is to be found everywhere. The only allusion he made to anything specific was in relation to the town sites. I have not the information desired at hand, and I fail to see what bearing it can have on the cost of the prairie section, which was the subject under discussion, but if further information be desired on the town sites, no doubt my hon. colleague, the Minister of the Interior, will be able to give all the information necessary, which will show that whatever was done in that connection as between the-government and the company was entirely justified. My hon. friend said, and it has been repeatedly said in the debate, that the government are lifting-to use his expression-90 per cent of the load in this matter. That is an entire misapprehension of the situation, but we will come to that later on, and I shall not take up time by dwelling on it now. The conversations we had with respect to the cost of labour and railway ties and materials generally were not confined to any particular section, but had reference to the increased cost of the-road generally. I shall bring down information later, and in that respect I think

the request of my hon. friend was fair and reasonable. But I do not agree that it is of the utmost importance, though it may be of interest, to us to know what sums other roads have cost. I do not think there is any prairie road which pretends to be of the same character as the Grand Trunk Pacific. If some other company has built for less money, that will be no evidence whatever that this road is too expensive. If the claim is made that it is too expensive, that must be established by other reasons than by what some other road of a different character may have cost. My hon. friend asks, am I satisfied this road has cost $34,000 or $35,000 per mile. I know only one way of being satisfied that the road has cost that much, and that is by our engineer's report. Every statement of cost by the company is referred to the government engineer, Mr. Schreiber. Mr. Schreiber cannot watch the construction of the line everywhere, but he has his own officers supervising it, and they report to him. And if they tell him, and if he tells us, that these figures, supplied by the company, represent fairly the cost of that road, I-being an innocent sort of a person-would be satisfied that the statement is a fair and proper one. If any other information be obtained, depend on it, I shall be very glad to lay it before the House, but I should think that information of the character I have mentioned might be accepted by the House as evidence that this road is costing that money and costing it intelligently and honestly. And if hon. gentlemen can be satisfied on that point, I do not think it matters what some other road of some other-kind, built at a different time, actually cost.

What is it that Mr. Schreiber certifies to? Mr. Schreiber is an engineer. I do not know the modus operands but there aie different ways of getting at the cost. Mr. Schreiber makes his annual or semi-annual or quarterly journeys over the road. He looks particularly after its engineering features as an engineer naturally would. But does he examine the accounts? Does he in any way look into the contracts and sub-contracts and contracts under these again? Does he look into the cost of material? Does he look into what is paid and compare the cost with the current prices? These are things that a business man, detailed to look into the question of cost, would do, but I do not take it that such is Mr. Schreiber's duty. He has certain figures placed before him. He finds that so much has been spent on labour, so much on material, so much on something else. He sees the vouchers, but does he get underneath all that in a business sense to find out whether there have been extravagant sums paid or not. The mere fact of a man look-Mr. FIELDING.
ing as an engineer, after the engineering features of a road, its curves, its masonry, ',its culverts, and things of that kind, does not enable him to give an opinion as to the reasonableness of its cost. Does he do anything more than simply look at the vouchers placed in his hands and take the amounts there given as having gone into the different kinds of work, sum up the tctal, and then spread it over the mileage at so much per mile. Yet underneath all that there may be all sorts of extravagance, double payments, sub-contracts and the like, and the engineer would know nothing about them. It does not seem to me that it is his business to know because he is not sent there for that purpose. If he does not do what I have indicated he does not, then we have no certainty at all, even with Mr. Schreiber's certificate, that $35,000 peT mile have gone into the work. I notice a letter from Mr. Bell. I think Mr. Bell is an auditor. I know nothing to his discredit, what I do know of him i3 .entirely to his credit, and I have no desire to pass any reflection on him, but Mr. Schreiber says to Mr. Bell: ' What about these accounts? ' And Mr. Bell says: ' I have gone through the accounts and examined the vouchers.' What does that show? It shows that bills have been paid and the vouchers produced. But does Mr. Bell go into the question of proper cost and all these other questions which would establish extravagance or otherwise in the construction of the road? Possibly he may, but I imagine that what he does is to examine the accounts and see whether they have been paid and whether the vouchers are all right. If that is Mr. Bell's work, there is something underneath it all that may not have come out, and what makes me suspicious is the extraordinary high cost. The Finance Minister says you cannot compare one road with another unless you have similar conditions. That is true; 'out I am bound to suppose that neither the Canadian Pacific or the Canadian Northern are running sheep paths up through that country. I think they are building good roads, and I am told that their grades and curves and road-beds, if not equal, are very nearly equal to those of this road. Of course, roads are always getting better where properly cared for; but when you come to compare $18,000 with $35,000 a mile, you have a very large margin for extra ballasting and improving curves and grades. I am told that the hauling capacity of the Canadian Pacific Railway and Canadian Northern is just about as great as that of this road.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Mr. Schreiber was here until a short time ago, when I released him from attendance, not supposing that he would be required. All the matters men-

tioned by my hon. friend are part of the engineering, because it is the duty of an engineer to report that a certain work is going to cost a certain sum, which necessarily implies that he must pass judgment on the reasonableness of the charges for labour, rails, ties, &c. Therefore I think it is reasonable to suppose that Mr. Sehrei-ber, in making his certificates and estimates, assisted by Mr. Bell, a very expert auditor, who examines all the vouchers, does look into all these matters, and the certificate he gives is to be accepted as reasonable evidence that the road will actually cost the sum he mentions in his report, and we are disposed to accept it in that light. But before the matter comes up again, I will discuss these points with him.
Who is Mr. Bell ?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The auditor of the government Railway Department.
Would the minister also bring down a statement as to the cuts and valleys ?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I couid not answer as to that.
Would the minister tell us when the first conference took place which led up to the negotiations for this loan between the government and the company ?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I think I would not know.

I think the Finance Minister must know; if not, the Prime Minister would know. I think the House would be pleased to have xurther information about it, in view of the circumstances surrounding this whole transaction.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: My hon. friend should not trust his imagination so lar.

There is a good deal more than imagination in it. The very fact that $7,000,000 of this money is going to the Grand Trunk Railway Company, and that it took such an active part in the election, and that a government running an election generally wants funds, and that within fifteen or twenty days after the election we have this letter from Mr. Hays stating that unless this is done the work is going to stop and financial ruin is going to stare us in the face and injure the financial status of Canada, causes suspicion that all the preliminary arrangements were made before the election, with the understanding that the scheme would be carried out after the elections in the event of the government being returned to power. Therefore we are interested in getting what information the government can give us about it, and I am quite sure that if they are willing to give it they are in a position to give it.
The hon. gentleman says something about the activity of the Grand Trunk during the last election. Let him tell us something about the activity of the officials of the Grand Trunk Pacific in the west.
I am talking to the Minister of Finance, who can give us the information we Tequire.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The only information I can give as to the activity of the Grand Trunk Pacific in support of the government, is that I heard very much the other way. But these things are not business.
Will the hon. minister tell us where he got his contributions ?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: My hon. friend has neglected his opportunities of testing all these things in the election courts, which is the proper place, and not here.
I understand the hon. minister to say that Mr. Schreiber has had resident engineers traversing this work, who are expected to know every thing that has been done.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I understand that Mr. Schreiber has had some inspection of the work; I have the impression that Mr. Schreiber had some officials acting for him in his absence.

I have no doubt that that is the case, and if so, these officials must have reported from time to time that the amount of money expended on wie road was very much in excess of the estimate, and the minister has been for some time in possession of that information.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes, we have known it for some time.
Then the hon. gentleman has had for some time the means for coming to the conclusion to come to the assistance of the company ?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
We had that only a
short time ago.
How long ago was the minister asked formally to come to the relief of the company ?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I do not remember.

It is a strange thing about the letter of November 16 that it drops, so to speak, from the clouds, an absolutely finished document and never since then does there seem to have been exchanged a single word altering its tenor.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Why should it be altered?
The resolution is drawn absolutely along the line of the letter. When the letter was written had an affirmative reply been promised to the writer?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I could not answer, I do not think it had. So far as I am concerned it had not.
How long'before the 16th of November had the substance of that letter been matters of pour parlers?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I could not answer; the letter will have to speak for itself-that is the value of the letter.
The letter does not say how long prior to that date the matter had been the subject of discussion between the minister and the authorities of the Grand Trunk Pacific.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I could not tell.
The minister would not have us erroneously believe that this letter suddenly fell upon him without any prior intimation?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It did not fall anywhere, it came in the ordinary way of business.
Absolutely unexpected?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I do not know as to that. We probably have expectations of these things sometimes.
Did the Minister of Finance draft it?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No, is it good enough for that?
Did the minister revise the letter before it was signed?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: My hon. friend is asking too many questions.

Any government going to the people does not v ant to conceal anything or exaggerate anything, it wants to put all the issues before the people. If the minister knew before October 26 that this $10,000,000 was looming in the air, does he think he did right towards the electors of Canada in not apprising them of the fact and getting their assent to it? It would have made a lovely refrain' to the cry of * Let Laurier finish his work ' if the Minister of Finance and the Prime Minister had told us what they knew, that $10,000,000 more had to be borrowed for the purpose? There is a great responsibility on the Minister of Finance in this matter. If he knew it, he did not deal rightly by the people and has no mandate from them; the hon. gentleman cught to go back and get a mapdate for a matter so important as this. If he did not know, the difficulty is to understand how this letter could have dropped out, fully finished, from the clouds, meeting exactly the view of the minister, because he has taken no objection to it from the first. I never knew of any proposition that did not have two sides to it, propositions and counter propositions.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: A bolt from the blue?

As though an all-wise Creator had moulded it. It was perfect. It fitted exactly the views of my hon. friend the Minister of Finance and Mr. Hays, and the only people it does not seem to fit are the public of Canada who have to pay for it.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: We do not agree with you there; we think it suits them.
Who constituted the company referred to by the Minister of Railways in a speech prior to the elections, when it was rumoured that the Grand Trunk Pacific were going to throw up the contract?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I have no recollection, I do not think I heard of it.
What is the character of the bridges and trestles?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I leave that to the engineers.
Will the minister get that information?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I will consider it.
Perhaps he had better do more than that.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: All I can do is to consider it.
It would be wiser to do more. All he has to do is to find out the nature of the bridges and trestles, whether the bridges and trestles are of steel and the culverts of stone or wood.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: If my hon. friend will put a specific question I will endeavour to get the information.
I put a specific question in each case.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Very good, we will consider it.
Would the minister endeavour to obtain for us some evidence that will enable him to convince us that this is really a superior road? That is readily reduced to a question of profile and figures.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is a fair question; I appreciate it.

We want to know about the grades, the curves and the character of the structures. Would it be possible for the minister to deal with the question raised in order that the House shall be permitted, either now or at some future date, to examine the statement containing the list of vouchers that go to make up the $35,000 per mile and that the House through one of its committees would be able to examine and take evidence to satisfy itself that the money has gone into the road?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I cannot answer that off-hand.
He will take that into consideration?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes.

Will he undertake to show what has been done with the 20 per cent payment on 10,000 shares of stock. We have been told that it went to the general purposes of the road. We would like something more specific. Where has it gone into the road and what is there to show for it? Would he also take up more definitely than has already been done, what will be the probable fixed charges in respect to capital investment for construction and to provide for what rolling stock has been placed on the road, what will be the fixed charges by way of interest on that section of the road and how these fixed charges will compare with the Canadian Northern and the Canadian Pacific Railway which run parallel to this road? It is a very important question because it will enable us to judge whether this company will be in a position to compete in grain rates or will be an active influence in keeping up grain rates.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: If the roads are of different character I do not think such a comparison will be of much value. Of course if a better road is given, as we claim, it will have such increased hauling power that even although the fixed charges are more it will still be a profitable road.
It will still be a question of degree and of comparison.

The three roads, the Grand Trunk Pacific, the Canadian Northern and the Canadian Pacific Railway run through similar country. Each road may be perfectly level for a long distance and then there may be a short grade of 4-10 per cent on the Grand Trunk Pacific and of 5-10 or 6-10 on the Canadian Northern Railway or the Canadian Pacific Railway. In order to have the comparison a fair one, would the minister have his engineers state both in miles and in number the grades on the different roads?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I think the committee and the House are entitled to the fullest information as to the superior character of this road and any possible information on that question I shall endeavour to get. As to comparisons with other roads, that is a different proposition and we will have to hold it in reserve.
What steps are being taken by the Grand Trunk Pacific to provide their share of the funds for the construction of the mountain section?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: They have some money in hand, as shown in the information supplied.
The minister cannot tell us off-hand how much money they have exclusively for the mountain section ?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I think the figures are in the printed statement, to which I would refer the hon. member (Mr. Ames).
Would it be pressing the matter too far if I asked whether any intimation has been given that further assistance of this character will be required regarding the mountain section ?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No such intimation has been received. Possibly, my hon. friend's suggestion that further assistance will be required may prove to be correct, but I have no such information now.

I can believe it to be quite nkely that the railway company will come to the government again, inasmuch as they can borrow at a very much lower rate of interest from the government than they can by floating bonds. I would like to ask also: Whore is the preferred stock today-has it been issued?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: If that is not covered by the information already brought down, 1 will have to ask the hon. member to leave the question for further consideration.
It is not in this information. The question is what has been done under their right to issue $20,000,000 of preferred stock ?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I will have that looked into.

It would be interesting also if the minister could tell us who compose the Grand Trunk Pacific Town Site Company, how much land they purchased, from whom they purchased it, what they paid for it, and how much of that money went to the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company. Also, who compose the Grand Trunk Pacific Construction Company, and lxow much of the road is under contract to them ?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I will look into that matter and see if I can get the information for my hon. friend.
Resolution reported, read the second time and concurred in.
Mr. FIELDING moved for leave to introduce Bill (No. 128) to authorize a loan to the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company.
I suppose the Bill will be printed at once and distributed ?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It is in print now, and I suppose the printing for members can be expedited.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: Motion agreed to, and Bill read the first time.

speakerposition: topic
Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: In moving the adjournment of the House, 1 may state that a desire has been expressed by hon. members on both sides, that if we dispose of this business to-night, the House might not find it necessary to meet to-morrow. The government have every disposition to concur in that suggestion. But His Excellency the Governor General will attend to-morrow in the Senate Chamber to assent to the Supply Bill and other Bills that are ready, and it will be necessary ior a sufficient number of members to be present to attend His Excellency. I would suggest that it might be agreed to have the House meet pro forma for the purpose indicated, but that, by common consent, no other business be taken up. It is hoped that such hon. members as remain in town will attend the pro-forma sitting in order that there may be a respectable quorum to respond to the knock of Black Rod.

Can the Minister of Finance do one thing more ? I understand that a return has been called for with reference to the indirect liabilities of the government, which return was to be presented to-morrow afternoon. Can this be rendered available before we adjourn ?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I think the information is available. If it be possible, we will have it brought down. Failing that, I will send it to the hon. gentleman during the recess.

Many hon. members wish to leave town to-morrow morning before the House is called. May I ask the hon. Minister of Finance if it may be understood that to-morrow shall not be a session of the House so that it will not tell against the members in their fifteen days' allowance.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Whatever my disposition is, I am afraid I have not the power to assent to that suggestion.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: Motion agreed to, and House adjourned at 11.25 p.m.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: Wednesday, April 7, 1909.
